pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–8 (UK Y3, US Grade 3). Recall and use multiplication AND division facts for the 3, 4 and 8 tables — the second fact set, exploiting the doubling chain 2→4→8.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3 'recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 3, 4 and 8 multiplication tables'. (By end of Y4 all tables to 12×12 memorised.)
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.7 'fluently multiply and divide within 100; by end of Grade 3 know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers'.
• Operational details: derive the 4s by doubling the 2s and the 8s by doubling the 4s (the doubling chain 2→4→8, banked from Counting & Cardinality skip counting); build 3s from counting-in-3s patterns and known facts; use commutativity and inverse to get four facts from one. Include division facts and out-of-order recall, not chanting.
• Checkpoint: recall + derive. Tier A (7): recall 3s and 4s facts in order. Tier B (7–8): recall any 3, 4 or 8 fact out of order and its division fact. Tier C (8): derive an 8s fact by doubling the matching 4s fact and explain the chain 2→4→8.
bestPractices: Build the 4s as doubles of the 2s and the 8s as doubles of the 4s — the doubling chain 2→4→8 — so the hardest of these tables (8s) is anchored to easier known facts and can be re-derived.
Learn division facts alongside multiplication as fact families and use commutativity, so one fact delivers four (4×8, 8×4, 32÷8, 32÷4).
Use the multiplication square and hundred-square patterns (3s make a diagonal stripe; 4s and 8s are doubled columns) to see the facts as a connected, patterned web rather than three isolated lists.
Rehearse out of order and in mixed problems to reach genuine recall, working toward the end-of-Y4 goal of all facts to 12×12.
Give the 8s the most rehearsal (weakest independent pattern of the three) and always tie a forgotten 8s fact back to 'double the 4s' as the repair strategy.
keyRepresentations: Multiplication square / times-table grid (patterns and commutative symmetry)
Doubling-chain number lines (2s → 4s → 8s, each jump doubling)
Arrays for each fact and its fact family
Hundred square with 3s, 4s, 8s shaded (diagonal / doubled-column patterns)
commonMisconceptions: Chanting a table but being unable to recall a fact out of order or its division fact.
Learning 4s and 8s as unrelated lists and not noticing 8s are doubled 4s — so a forgotten 8s fact can't be repaired.
Treating a×b and b×a as separate facts (not using commutativity).
Confusing adjacent tables (3s with 4s, 4s with 8s) because the steps feel similar.
Doubling errors when deriving 8s from 4s (adding instead of doubling, or doubling the wrong term).

learn.summary: For ages 7–8 (UK Y3, US Grade 3): recall and use multiplication AND division facts for the 3, 4 and 8 times tables, exploiting the doubling chain 2→4→8 so the hardest table (8s) is anchored to easier facts and can be re-derived. Teach division alongside multiplication as fact families (one fact gives four), rehearse out of order, and treat a forgotten 8s fact as a chance to repair via 'double the 4s'.

activities.title: The doubling chain: 2s → 4s → 8s
feedback: If a child treats 8s as a separate list and counts from zero, ring every other multiple of 4 to reveal the 8s and make the doubling relationship explicit.
If a child adds instead of doubles, or doubles the wrong term, pause on one array and physically double it so the operation is visible.
On any 8s miss, respond not with the bare answer but with 'what's the matching 4s fact? now double it.'
activities.rationale: Anchoring the 8s to the 4s (and 4s to the 2s) via doubling gives a repair strategy that survives a forgotten fact; manipulable arrays make the doubling concrete. Linking tables on a shared grid shows them as a patterned structure rather than lists to chant.
sourceClaims: 4s are derived by doubling 2s and 8s by doubling 4s (the doubling chain); the 8s need the most rehearsal and should be anchored to the 4s.
learnerActions: Pick a 2s fact such as 3×2=6 and build it as an array (3 rows of 2).
Double the array to make 3×4=12, then double again to make 3×8=24, saying aloud 'double the 2s gives the 4s; double the 4s gives the 8s'.
Repeat the chain for several facts (e.g. 7×2=14 → 7×4=28 → 7×8=56), each time predicting the next fact before doubling.
When an 8s fact is forgotten, recover it by finding the matching 4s fact and doubling it (e.g. forgot 3×8 → find 3×4=12 → double → 24).

Shade the 3s, 4s and 8s on a hundred square (or read their rows on a multiplication square): on the hundred square, notice that the multiples of 3 make diagonal stripes, and on either grid notice that the 8s multiples are every other 4s multiple.
activities.intendedInsight: The 8s table, usually the hardest, is 'just double the 4s, which are double the 2s'. Facts are a connected, patterned web, not three isolated lists, so a forgotten fact can be rebuilt.

activities.title: One fact gives four: multiplication and division fact families
feedback: If division is noticeably slower than multiplication, return to the fact-family triangle and read every × fact together with its two ÷ facts.
If a child treats a×b and b×a as separate facts, rotate the array a quarter-turn to show it is the same quantity.
Prompt: 'What's 32÷8, and which multiplication fact helped you?'
activities.rationale: Learning division alongside multiplication as fact families and using commutativity builds genuine recall economically and closes the common gap where division trails multiplication.
sourceClaims: Y3: recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 3, 4 and 8 multiplication tables; by end of Y4 all tables to 12×12 memorised.
3.OA.7 fluently multiply and divide within 100 and know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers by end of Grade 3.
learnerActions: Take one fact such as 4×8=32 and write its whole family: 4×8=32, 8×4=32, 32÷8=4, 32÷4=8.
Use a fact-family triangle (32 at top, 4 and 8 below) to read off each of the four facts, covering a corner to find the missing number.
Build the same family as an array and re-read it two ways (4 rows of 8, 8 rows of 4) to see commutativity.
Practise the division facts until they are as quick as the multiplication facts, e.g. given 24÷8, name the × fact you used (3×8=24).
activities.intendedInsight: Commutativity and the inverse relationship mean one known fact delivers four; division need not lag behind multiplication.

activities.title: Out-of-order recall and targeting the sticky facts
feedback: If errors cluster on the hard facts while easy ones are fluent, do NOT mass-drill the whole table — target those few facts with derivation and spaced retrieval.
Confusing related tables (3s with 4s, 4s with 8s): slow down and check with one array, by counting on one step, or (for 4s and 8s) by doubling or halving.
Celebrate a correct derivation as highly as a recalled fact — both show a secure, networked grasp.
activities.rationale: Out-of-order and mixed practice reaches genuine recall rather than chant-dependent sequencing; targeting hard facts with derivation and spaced retrieval is more efficient than undifferentiated drill. This supports the end-of-Y4 goal of all tables to 12×12.
sourceClaims: Y3: recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 3, 4 and 8 multiplication tables; by end of Y4 all tables to 12×12 memorised.
4s are derived by doubling 2s and 8s by doubling 4s (the doubling chain); the 8s need the most rehearsal and should be anchored to the 4s.
learnerActions: Answer mixed 3s/4s/8s facts in random order (both × and ÷), noting which you recalled instantly and which you had to work out.
Identify your few hardest facts (often the high ones like 4×7, 8×6, 8×7) and rehearse just those with spaced repetition rather than re-chanting the whole table.
Derive a sticky fact from partial products, e.g. 8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2 = 40 + 16 = 56, or 8×6 as double 4×6 (24→48).
Fill the blank in fact families and match a given fact to the correct array.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means recalling or efficiently deriving any fact out of order, with effort concentrated on the few genuinely hard facts, not mass-drilling what is already known.

constraints: The learning target is recalled facts: timed/mixed recall exercises check fluency but do not by themselves build the doubling structure — pair them with array building and the doubling chain.

A static multiplication-square or hundred-square poster is a strong reference and pattern-shower but cannot run out-of-order recall or animate the doubling; use it as a support alongside active practice.

Oral quiz-partner drill offers rehearsal and can verbally prompt the 'double the 4s' repair on an 8s miss, but talking alone does not display an array doubling in size; pair it with a visual array where you want the relationship seen.
Division facts must be rehearsed to the same security as multiplication; left implicit they tend to lag.
When using paper arrays or counters, remember they approximate the abstract fact; the point is the number relationship, not the physical objects themselves.

Interactive aids that recolour the grid, pop an array on tapping a cell, or animate an array doubling in size are helpful optional ways to make the mechanism visible — they are examples, not requirements.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent final re-review performed: the prior reviewer's empty unresolved list was not trusted. Confirmed the DfE topic claim is correctly absent from the doubling-chain activity (its rationale rests on the NCETM doubling principle) and the oral quiz-partner constraint is rescoped to a narrow affordance. No fresh source verification was carried out.

The source marks the UK National Curriculum claim as verified; the CCSS 3.OA.7 claim and the NCETM doubling-chain claim are marked unverified in the source — treat their evidence strength as unconfirmed.

Out-of-order recall and spaced retrieval (activity 3) derive from the pedagogy best-practice notes; among the cited claims, the DfE claim directly supports the end-of-Y4 all-tables goal and the NCETM claim supports giving the 8s the most rehearsal, while the fact-family/commutativity principle in activity 2 is a pedagogy-note principle not directly carried by any sources[].claim.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3×8=24, 4×7=28, 8×6=48 (double 24), 3×9=27, 32÷8=4, 24÷3=8, 28÷4=7, 24÷8=3, 8×7=56 (40+16) all check out and were retained as stated. The '27' in the source correctAnswer corresponds to 3×9 from the diagnostic prompt.

The original source expressed comparative/necessity framing (e.g. that 3D 'adds no value' and that posters/quizzes/conversation can only support or test, not teach). These have been softened to scoped, observable affordances/limits rather than universal laws, since the source ratings do not establish comparative efficacy.

probeDeeper: What's 32 ÷ 8, and which × fact did you use?
Which fact is hardest for you?
assess.correctAnswer: 28, 48, 27; 4, 8, 7; and 8 × 6 is double 4 × 6 (24 → 48). Facts recalled or efficiently derived, with division as secure as multiplication.

errorPatterns.pattern: isolated facts, no derivation — knows some 4s but treats the 8s as a separate list, unable to use 4 × 6 to reach 8 × 6
errorPatterns.nextMove: teach doubling (8 = double 4) and ring every other multiple of 4 to reveal the 8s; make the relationship explicit
errorPatterns.revealedBy: cannot connect 4s and 8s; laboriously counts the 8s from zero

errorPatterns.pattern: high facts are the weak spots — reliable on easy ones, slow or guessing on 4 × 7, 8 × 6, 8 × 7
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT mass-drill the whole table — target the few sticky facts with derivation (8 × 7 = 8 × 5 + 8 × 2) and spaced retrieval
errorPatterns.revealedBy: errors concentrate on the known-hard facts while easy facts are fluent

errorPatterns.pattern: division facts lag — quick on × but slow on 32 ÷ 8
errorPatterns.nextMove: use fact-family triangles linking each × fact to its two ÷ facts

responseLevels.gap: Cannot recall 3/4/8 facts and counts each from zero with errors.
responseLevels.full: Recalls 3/4/8 multiplication and division facts fluently and derives harder ones (8s from 4s, 8 × 7 from partial products).
responseLevels.partial: Recalls the easier facts but the high 7×/8× and division facts are slow or reconstructed, with little use of doubling.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Quick-fire, and tell me if you had to work any out: 4 × 7? 8 × 6? 3 × 9? Then the divisions: 32 ÷ 8? 24 ÷ 3? 28 ÷ 4? And one more — how could knowing 4 × 6 help you find 8 × 6? (Watch recall versus derivation, the harder 7×/8× facts, and whether they use doubling.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 3/4/8 tables are harder, and the 'use 4 × 6 to get 8 × 6' prompt tests whether facts are networked (doubling links 4s and 8s) or held as isolated lists. Errors clustering on the high 7×/8× facts, and weaker division, mark a fragile grasp.
